what.a: {brand} (Bamboo Cicada), also called pull-string cicada, is a traditional folk toy that chirps when spun. This page is a zero-dependency web simulation of it — the {cyber} that netizens call it — and works directly in mobile and desktop browsers.

howToPlay.step1: Press and hold the bamboo stick on the screen.
howToPlay.step2: Swing it in a circle; the faster it spins, the louder and quicker it chirps.
howToPlay.step3: You can also tap “Auto Spin”, or use the “Shake Phone” motion mode on supported phones.

howItWorks.a: The real toy connects the bamboo membrane and stick with a rosin-coated string. When swung, the rosin string undergoes stick-slip friction; the vibration travels to the membrane and is amplified by the bamboo tube cavity. This simulation uses rope-and-particle physics, Canvas 2D, and Web Audio, prioritizing real Zhuzhiliao recording samples.

compatibility.a: Works in modern desktop and mobile browsers, requiring JavaScript, HTML5 Canvas, and Web Audio. The phone motion mode requires HTTPS or a local file and may need motion sensor permission; when WebGL is unavailable it automatically falls back to 2D.

faq.title: FAQ
faq.q1: Do I need to download or install anything?
faq.a1: No. The page has no build step or dependencies — just open it in a browser. The main page can also be saved and opened offline.
faq.q2: Why is there no sound the first time?
faq.a2: Browsers usually require a user click or touch before playing sound; tap the page or “Tap to enable sound” to unlock it.
faq.q3: Why can’t I use the Shake Phone mode?
faq.a3: This mode relies on motion sensors, requires HTTPS or a local file, and iPhone may need permission on first use.
faq.q4: What kind of toy is Zhuzhiliao?
faq.a4: Zhuzhiliao is a traditional Chinese folk toy, also known regionally as Bamboo Cicada or pull-string cicada. A bamboo tube is covered with a membrane at one end; a rosin-coated string is tied to the center of the membrane and to a small bamboo stick at the other end. When you hold the stick and swing it in circles, the string stick-slips on the rosin, vibrating the membrane, and the bamboo cavity amplifies it into a cicada-like “wah-wah” sound.
faq.a5: “Cyber Zhuzhiliao” is the nickname netizens gave to this kind of web simulation: instead of buying a real bamboo toy, you press and spin in the browser to hear the exact same “wah-wah” sound, taken from real Zhuzhiliao recordings.
faq.a6: Completely free, no ads, no in-app purchases, no registration; the code is open source on GitHub.
faq.q7: Is the sound synthesized or a real recording?
faq.a7: The main source is a real Zhuzhiliao recording sample, with playback rate driven by spin speed; only when the sample fails to decode does it fall back to Web Audio synthesis.
faq.a8: Yes. A Service Worker caches core resources, and you can “Install” it to the desktop as a PWA.
faq.a9: Only anonymous site-wide wah counts, visits, and online users are counted; your personal wah count is stored only in the browser locally, with no personal identity information collected.

sources.title: Author & Sources
sources.desc: The page’s audio source is field-recorded by the author from a real Zhuzhiliao toy; the physics model is implemented from measured proportions of the real object, and the code is fully open source.

noscript.title: What is Zhuzhiliao?
noscript.p1: Zhuzhiliao, known in many places as Bamboo Cicada or pull-string cicada, is a traditional folk toy that chirps “wah-wah” when spun: a bamboo tube is covered with a membrane, a rosin-coated string ties the membrane center to a small bamboo stick. Hold the stick and swing in circles — the string stick-slips on the rosin, vibration travels to the membrane, and the bamboo cavity amplifies it into that cicada-like “wah—wah—”.
noscript.p2: This is its web simulation, the “Cyber Zhuzhiliao”: press and spin on the screen; the faster it spins, the louder it gets, with sound from real Zhuzhiliao recordings. Free, ad-free, open source — requires JavaScript to play.
